newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asian Gold - Eye on physical demand, U.S. rates.
newsitem.headline: Asian Gold - Eye on physical demand, U.S. rates.

text.p: Steady regional physical demand and U.S. interest rates were the only talking points in Asian markets that saw little else affecting gold prices in the short term, Hong Kong and Singapore dealers said on Friday.
Physical demand continued at a steady clip providing support to gold prices, Asian dealers said.
"The premium on tael gold remains firm, which indicates to me demand from China is fairly strong," said a senior bullion dealer in Hong Kong.
A Hong Kong jeweller said that demand from mainland tourists visiting the territory remained healthy.
High taxes pushed gold prices on the mainland to about 4,450 yuan per tael, or US$536 per tael, compared to Hong Kong prices at $352.40/90 per tael.
"It's almost a 30 to 70 percent divide, with mainland customers buying most of the gold," said a source at a large local jewellery firm.
Singapore dealers concurred, noting that physical gold demand remained firm in China and the rest of northern Asia.
They said buying in Indonesia slowed down because of the recent fluctuations in the rupiah, precious metal dealers said.

"I heard Chinese buying is going very well," a dealer for a North American bank in Singapore said. "But the Indonesians are taking a look at the market first after the recent movements in the rupiah."
Another Singapore dealer said demand from areas like Malaysia and Hong Kong had been "reasonably good."
Singapore premiums over spot London prices eased slightly to 130-140 U.S. cents from last week's 140-150 cents due to a lingering shortage of high-grade gold kilobars in the city-state.
"There is a shortage of kilobars and we are a bit puzzled by the situation," a dealer for a bank in Singapore said.
"There's no sign of the shortage easing and that's why premiums have remained at their current levels."
Gold was seen trading in a range between US$348-$354 an ounce in the coming week with buyers likely to become plentiful if the yellow metal slipped below $350 per ounce.
"When the market goes further away from $350, the buying begins to dry up. We see more buyers when gold begins to approach $350 or slips below that," one dealer said.
In the absence of any other notable market-moving factors, dealers turned to U.S. interest rate issues as possibly nudging gold out of the doldrums.
"Gold is a bit stuck at the moment," said one Hong Kong source.
U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan signalled on Thursday that the central bank could raise interest rates, possibly as soon as next week.

"If the interest rates increase maybe half a percent or more, the Dow (Jones Industrial Average) will continue its slide and gold will have a real chance to pop up five or six dollars, and that'll just get it out of this scary little area," another senior bullion dealer in Hong Kong said.
"Once it breaks above $355 and $356, you can start a new range back in the $357-362 area," he said.
Asian gold market were simply looking for direction from other markets, another source said.

-- Rene Pastor, Singapore Newsroom (65-8703305)
